name: Marketing / Strategic Communication
hook: Students generate ten campaigns in an hour, then have to defend why nine of them are bad.

make.body: Physical packaging or a point-of-sale piece for a real local client. Holding a mockup surfaces every decision a slide deck hides: size, weight, what the customer reads first from arm’s length.

build.body: A message-testing harness. Students generate a wide spread of positioning variants, then build a simple landing page per variant and measure. The AI supplies volume; the student supplies the judgment about which variant is worth defending.

plan.txt: Land one real client, even a campus organization. Written brief, signed by the client — enough to design the packaging or point-of-sale mockup from.
Submit the packaging cut file at the start of the week. Generate wide with AI in class, then cut down to three positions with a written rationale per cut.
Build one page per position, run whatever traffic is available for five days.
Client presentation with the physical mockup and the actual numbers. The client picks. Students debrief the gap between their favorite and the client’s.

prompt: Generate twelve distinct positioning statements for this product, aimed at this audience: [describe product and audience]. Make them genuinely different from each other in strategy, not in wording: vary what need is being claimed, what the competition is, and what the customer has to believe. Number them. Then for each one, write the single sentence a skeptical customer would say to reject it.
tryTuesday: 90 minutes, one real client named at the start — a campus club works. Minutes 0–10: write the client's actual objective in one sentence. Minutes 10–40: run the twelve-positioning-statements prompt, then cut to three, writing a one-line rationale for every cut. Minutes 40–75: an arm's-length test — students show the three surviving positions to people from other majors and record which the stranger believed and which they distrusted on sight. Minutes 75–90: report the gap between the position the team liked and the one outsiders trusted. The deliverable is the cut rationale plus the arm's-length notes; it grades the judgment that survives after AI supplies the volume.

replaces.assignment: The semester campaign deck presented to the class.
replaces.lost: The polished, comprehensive campaign document and its production values.
replaces.gained: Students practice the actual professional move — killing nine plausible ideas and defending why — instead of over-investing in one campaign picked in week two; the grade rewards discrimination over decoration.

aiFailsHere: A model generates marketing copy that is fluent, on-trend, and strategically empty — converging on the same benefit language ('elevate', 'seamless', 'community') regardless of product, and asserting a differentiator without evidence any customer cares about it. Its output looks like a finished campaign while smuggling in unvalidated claims, some of which — health, sustainability — invite regulatory and skeptical scrutiny it never flags.

rubric.description: The retained positions rest on genuinely different bets — need, competitor, required belief — not reworded versions of one idea.
Each elimination is justified against the client's objective and audience, not the team's taste.
The arm's-length test is reported honestly, distinguishing what an outsider believed from what the team hoped.
Flags positions that depend on unproven or regulated claims before they anchor the campaign.

budget.perStudentCost: $0 for the Tuesday version; roughly $10–20 per team in print or cut stock for packaging or point-of-sale mockups in the four-week version.
budget.fileDueWeek: First day of Week 2 — submit the packaging cut file at the start of the week the positions are chosen; it is designed from the week-1 client brief. PACE quotes 7–10 business days (up to 14 calendar days), so it clears before the week-4 client presentation.
budget.calendarNote: Message testing needs no lead time. The packaging mockup is designed from the week-1 client brief, so its file goes in at the start of week 2 and the up-to-14-calendar-day turnaround clears before the week-4 client presentation.

scales.oneSession: The 90-minute generate-cut-test session producing a cut rationale and arm's-length notes; no fabrication.
scales.fourWeeks: The seeded four-week plan: signed client brief, wide generation cut to three, one landing page per position with real traffic, then a client presentation with the physical mockup and the numbers.
scales.oneSemester: A full client engagement — brief, wide generation, a multivariate landing-page test with real traffic, fabricated packaging, and a final debrief on the gap between the team's favorite and the client's choice.

promptOutput.model: Claude (Anthropic) — captured 2026-07-27 in an isolated fresh session with no build context; output is unedited.
promptOutput.promptFilled: Filled in as a Kakaʻako-brewed kombucha brand sold at farmers markets, aimed at health-conscious Honolulu office workers aged 25–45.
promptOutput.output:
Here are twelve positioning statements, each built on a different strategic bet, followed by the rejection each would earn from a skeptic.

**1. The energy play** — For office workers who hit an afternoon slump, our kombucha is the clean alternative to a third coffee that lifts you without the crash.
*Skeptic: "It's fizzy tea, not a stimulant — I'd feel nothing."*

**2. The gut-health play** — For people who care about digestion, our raw, unpasteurized brew delivers live cultures that a probiotic pill can't match.
*Skeptic: "A capsule is dosed and studied; your bottle is a guess."*

**3. The sugar-swap play** — For anyone quitting soda, we're the tart, bubbly drink that scratches the same itch for a fraction of the sugar.
*Skeptic: "Kombucha still has sugar — this is marketing, not a swap."*

**4. The local-provenance play** — For Honolulu residents who want to keep dollars on-island, we're the kombucha brewed a few blocks from your desk, not shipped from the mainland.
*Skeptic: "I care how it tastes, not the zip code it's brewed in."*

**5. The ritual play** — For the weekend farmers-market crowd, we're the small pleasure that makes Saturday morning feel intentional.
*Skeptic: "That's a vibe, not a reason to spend $9."*

**6. The status play** — For people whose desk drink signals their standards, we're what you're seen holding instead of a Red Bull.
*Skeptic: "Nobody at my office is judging my beverage."*

**7. The clean-label play** — For label-readers, we're the drink with five ingredients you can pronounce and nothing you can't.
*Skeptic: "Every brand claims that now — it's table stakes, not a difference."*

**8. The hydration play** — For desk-bound people who forget to drink water, we're the flavorful reason you'll actually stay hydrated all day.
*Skeptic: "Water is free and does that better."*

**9. The craft/flavor play** — For those bored by mass-market SKUs, we're the small-batch kombucha with rotating flavors you can't get anywhere else.
*Skeptic: "I found a flavor I like — I don't want it to disappear next month."*

**10. The immunity play** — For people trying not to get sick in a shared open-plan office, we're the daily habit that supports your defenses.
*Skeptic: "No drink has ever stopped me catching what's going around."*

**11. The mindful-alcohol play** — For happy-hour skippers, we're the sophisticated non-alcoholic pour that holds its own in a glass.
*Skeptic: "If I'm not drinking, I'll just have a soda water for free."*

**12. The values-community play** — For buyers who want their money to back real people, we're a brand you can meet face-to-face every weekend.
*Skeptic: "I like the founder, but I buy on price and taste, not friendship."*

A note: several of these (immunity, gut health) lean on claims that invite regulatory scrutiny and the sharpest skepticism — worth validating before they anchor your messaging.

annotations.marker: Genuine strategic diversity across the twelve
annotations.note: The energy, gut-health, sugar-swap, local-provenance and status plays rest on materially different bets — the model followed the 'different in strategy, not wording' instruction well.

annotations.marker: Self-flagged regulatory risk on immunity and gut-health claims
annotations.note: Unprompted, it warned that claims #2 and #10 'invite regulatory scrutiny' — a useful, accurate caution students should heed.

annotations.marker: Skeptic lines are real objections, not strawmen
annotations.note: 'Water is free and does that better' and 'that's a vibe, not a reason to spend $9' are the actual rejections these positions earn.

annotations.marker: Convergent phrasing: nearly every entry uses a 'For [people] who...' frame
annotations.note: The template repetition shows the model's pull toward one copy structure; a student should vary the form when testing so the frame itself is not the confound.

related.reason: Both generate a wide spread with AI and grade which few survive contact with a real audience, not the volume produced.
Both hand construction to AI so the graded work becomes defending the assumptions or claims the polished output quietly depends on.
